lens: facts and integrity: every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution in client/public/essays/why-does-god-allow-suffering.json checked against the claims ledger, the site's BSB text (client/public/bible/ch/) and 18 web searches (web pages themselves could not be opened: www.crossway.org, archive.spectator.co.uk and en.wikipedia.org do not resolve from this session, so matches rest on the text the search tool returned)

findings.where: ## What Job's Friends Got Wrong, third paragraph, first sentence: "When God finally speaks, he takes Job's side: "My anger burns against you and against your two friends, for you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7)."
findings.problem: (e) The quotation and reference are right, but the sentence gets the order of events in Job wrong. The verse itself begins "After the LORD had spoken these words to Job" (ESV; BSB Job 42:7 reads "After the LORD had spoken these words to Job, He said to Eliphaz"). God's first words from the whirlwind are a challenge to Job, not a vindication (Job 38:2, 40:2, 40:8). He sides with Job against the friends only after chapters 38 to 41. "When God finally speaks" makes 42:7 sound like God's first word in the book, and the next paragraph then goes back to the whirlwind speeches, so the order is reversed. A reader who knows Job will catch it. The ledger checks only the wording of 42:7, not this framing.
findings.fix: Replace "When God finally speaks, he takes Job's side:" with "In the end, God takes Job's side:". Leave the quotation and "(Job 42:7)" as they are.

findings.where: Opening section, second paragraph, second sentence: "A Jesuit preacher named Gabriel Malagrida published a pamphlet in 1756 insisting that the cause was not nature but the city's sins, and he called the city to penance."
findings.problem: (g) Restoration. The ledger records the writer's original, "urged Lisbon toward processions and penance before rebuilding". Earlier passes cut "processions" and "before rebuilding" because no source they saw supported them. This run's searches found a source for "before rebuilding": The Spectator, 27 April 1956, p. 28, "Apocalyptic", a review of T. D. Kendrick's The Lisbon Earthquake (Methuen, 1956). As the search tool returned it, the review says Malagrida urged the Portuguese to put religious exercises before reconstruction and that his exhortations increased public hysteria. The Wikipedia "Gabriel Malagrida" entry, as returned, adds that Carvalho was trying to rebuild Lisbon after the earthquake, which Malagrida preached was the punishment of a just God on a sinful people. Penance as the pamphlet's remedy is already in the ledger (USP: "sempre tem na penitencia o seu remedio"). Processions still appear in no source. Caveat: the review is a secondhand summary of Kendrick, seen only as search-result text, and the page could not be opened.
findings.fix: Change "and he called the city to penance." to "and he urged Lisbon toward penance before rebuilding." Keep "processions" out. Add a ledger line under Lisbon citing the Spectator review of Kendrick (27 April 1956, p. 28) and the Wikipedia Malagrida entry as seen by search on 2026-10-28. If the fixer wants a second independent source before restoring, keep the present wording, which is accurate.

findings.where: ## What Job's Friends Got Wrong, first paragraph: "Three friends come to comfort him, and the first thing they do is the wisest thing they do in the whole book: "And they sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights ..." (Job 2:13)."
findings.problem: (e) Close reading. Job 2:12 comes before the sitting: the friends weep aloud, tear their robes and throw dust on their heads (BSB 2:12 and 2:13). The sitting is the first thing they do before they speak, not strictly the first thing they do. The quotation and reference are correct.
findings.fix: Optional: "Three friends come to comfort him, and before they say anything they do the wisest thing they do in the whole book:" (rest of the sentence unchanged).

findings.where: ## Natural Evil and Animal Suffering, last paragraph: "Isaiah saw a day when the wolf will dwell with the lamb, and "They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain" (Isaiah 11:9)."
findings.problem: (e) The wolf-and-lamb line paraphrases Isaiah 11:6 without quotation marks, which is allowed. But the only reference in the sentence is 11:9, so a reader checking it may look for the wolf in 11:9. BSB confirms 11:6 ("The wolf will live with the lamb") and 11:9.
findings.fix: Optional: "Isaiah saw a day when the wolf will dwell with the lamb (Isaiah 11:6), and "They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain" (Isaiah 11:9)."

findings.where: ## Natural Evil and Animal Suffering, second paragraph: "Many read Genesis 3 and Romans 5:12 to mean that death of every kind, animal death included, entered the world through human sin, and most of them hold that the earth is young."
findings.problem: (a) The clause "most of them hold that the earth is young" has no ledger line of its own. The ledger line covers only the two readings, stated and left open. The clause is a characterization, not a figure, and it is sound: holding that no animal died before the fall, alongside the fossil record, nearly requires a young earth. Old-earth exceptions such as the retroactive-fall view are a minority. There is still nothing in the ledger behind it.
findings.fix: No change to the essay text. Add a ledger line under "A creation that groans" recording the clause as a general characterization with no statistic claimed. If the fixer prefers no unledgered claim, cut ", and most of them hold that the earth is young".

findings.where: Ledger docs/work/essays/ledgers/why-does-god-allow-suffering.md, the opening words of the lines for the Lisbon fires, the Lisbon tsunami, Kushner, "Dozens of psalms" and Eric Wolterstorff
findings.problem: (c) Ledger housekeeping, not an essay error. Several lines still open with the superseded, generalized wording, for example "Fires 'broke out across the city and burned for days'", "His son Aaron had progeria ... and died young", "'Many psalms are complaints addressed straight to God.'" and "His son Eric died young in a climbing accident". The restoration to the essay's present wording is recorded only further down each line. The essay matches the restorations, but a fixer skimming the line openings could restore the generalized text by mistake.
findings.fix: Begin each of those ledger lines with the essay's current wording (for example: "In 1983 his son Eric, twenty-five years old, died in a climbing accident in Austria.") and keep the history after it. No change to the essay.

clean_checks: Lisbon: November 1, 1755, All Saints' Day, morning, churches full for Mass, roofs on the worshipers: ledger verified (envoy's letter, McCabe, Houston).

"Within the hour a tsunami surged up the Tagus into the lower city": ledger restored. Search this run: Wikipedia about 40 minutes, a Lisbon site 45 minutes, NOAA about an hour, some accounts about 11 a.m. Low-lying Baixa flooded. "Within the hour" is the majority reading, so do not restore "About forty minutes later".
Fires from fallen candles and kitchen hearths burning for days where the water did not reach: ledger restored, with sources named. Matches the essay.

"Estimates of the dead still vary widely, into the tens of thousands": ledger generalization kept. Search this run again showed estimates from 10,000 to 60,000 and 30,000 to 50,000, so do not restore the writer's range.

Malagrida a Jesuit preacher; pamphlet 1756 (Juizo da verdadeira causa do terremoto); sins, not nature; penance: ledger verified. Search this run confirmed the 1756 pamphlet and "solely our intolerable sins".

Voltaire's poem against the philosophers of the best of all possible worlds; the children "crushed and bleeding on their mothers' breasts" (paraphrase, no quotation marks): ledger verified in McCabe. Search this run confirmed the French line "Sur le sein maternel écrasés et sanglants", so "crushed and bleeding" renders Voltaire's own words (McCabe has "bleeding and torn").
Rousseau: twenty thousand houses six or seven stories high (paraphrase, letter of 18 August 1756): ledger restored with the French "de six à sept étages". Matches.
Epicurus taught in Athens about 300 BC; the argument survives in nothing he wrote; usually credited to him: ledger verified (Diogenes Laertius X; Wikipedia Epicurean paradox).

Lactantius, a Christian teacher, early fourth century, treatise on the anger of God (313 to 314): ledger verified. The block quotation matches the ANF text word for word, as recorded by the ledger and confirmed by search this run (the epicureanfriends forum reproduction; the bkv.unifr.ch ANF text was in the results). The essay cites no chapter, so the chapter numbering that differs between editions does not matter.
Lactantius's own answer (wisdom and virtue grow by overcoming evils): paraphrase, ledger checked against the ANF.

Hume, Dialogues, Philo the skeptic: "Epicurus's old questions are yet unanswered." Ledger verified in Gutenberg #4583, Part X. Search this run returned the same wording. "Fourteen centuries later" ledger verified.

Plantinga's free will defense; strict contradiction; many on both sides, atheists among them (Mackie, 1982): ledger verified. The plain summary without quotation marks matches God, Freedom, and Evil p. 30 as the ledger records it. Plantinga is living, and the sentence is fair to him.

Rowe 1979, atheist, the fawn burned in a lightning fire, several days of agony, suffering that appears pointless "so far as we can see": ledger verified. Search this run returned the APQ 16.4 passage (p. 337) and Rowe's "so far as we can see" framing. The cut sentence ("No one sees it ...") correctly stays cut.

Darwin, letter to the botanist Asa Gray, 22 May 1860, Ichneumonidae feeding within living caterpillars, glossed as wasps: ledger verified in Life and Letters vol. II. "More than a century earlier" (1860 to 1979) is arithmetic.

Dostoevsky: The Brothers Karamazov published 1880 (serial completed November 1880; book issued December 1880); chapter "Rebellion"; the general's hounds and the eight-year-old serf boy before his mother; the five-year-old girl in the privy: ledger verified in Garnett #28054. The quotation "It's not God that I don't accept, Alyosha, only I most respectfully return Him the ticket." was re-seen by search this run in Garnett's wording. Dostoevsky as a believer: ledger verified (Baring).

Biography: "I came to faith as an adult, out of atheism" matches NOTES.md. "Baptists, my own tradition" is allowed, with no Southern Baptist claim. The ledger asks James to confirm he is comfortable with the stance in that sentence. That is a James sign-off, not a factual gap.

C. S. Lewis, The Problem of Pain, 1940; the fixed-laws argument and the close, unquoted paraphrase of "Try to exclude the possibility of suffering ... you find that you have excluded life itself": ledger verified. It is attributed and has no quotation marks.
Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon near the end of the second century; the mother-and-infant image (Against Heresies 4.38.1), paraphrased: ledger verified.

Augustine, Enchiridion 11: "if He were not so omnipotent and good that He can bring good even out of evil." Ledger verified in the NPNF. Search this run confirmed chapter 11 and the same English wording.

Joy Davidman died of cancer in July 1960 (13 July); A Grief Observed published under N. W. Clerk (1961): ledger verified. The three Lewis quotations match the HarperSanFrancisco text the ledger cites, punctuation included (comma inside "So there's no God after all,").

Job's losses (Job 1:2, 1:13-19), sores (2:7), three friends (2:11); Job 2:13, 4:7, 42:5 and 42:7 quoted in ESV form with references. BSB confirms each verse and its sense. Eliphaz in chapter 22 (22:6, 22:9) is a fair gloss: ESV says "the naked", the essay "the poor", with no quotation marks. 42:8 (Job prays for the friends) is right. The whirlwind questions (38:4, 38:39-41, 39:27-30) match the BSB. The heavenly court of chapters 1 and 2 is right (1:6-12, 2:1-6).
Luke 13:4-5 quotation (ESV, matched), with the Galileans and Pilate (13:1-2) and the eighteen at Siloam (13:4). John 9:2 quotation and 9:3, where Jesus rejects both options. BSB confirms all of them.

Kushner: Aaron diagnosed at three with progeria, a disease of rapid aging; died in 1977, two days after his fourteenth birthday; When Bad Things Happen to Good People, 1981; God wholly loving and just but limited in power; millions of readers (more than 4 million copies): ledger verified by several obituaries. Kushner died in 2023, so the closing critique is not about a living person, and it is a fair theological reading of his stated view.

Genesis 50:20 (ESV), the brothers after their father's death (50:15). Acts 2:23, both phrases from one verse, in Peter's Pentecost sermon. Romans 8:28 and 8:35. James 1:13. All in ESV form with references. BSB confirms the sense.

Westminster Confession 3.1, "neither is God the author of sin": ledger verified in Creeds.json. Reformed, Wesleyan and Arminian characterizations: ledger verified (Wesley Sermon 67; Arminius; Olson). Baptists on both sides since the seventeenth century (1611 and 1644 confessions): ledger verified. The question is left open, with no position asserted for James.

Romans 8:20-22 block quotation, 8:23 and 8:26 in ESV form. The gloss "when we don't know how to pray" (no quotation marks) matches the sense (BSB "we do not know how we ought to pray"). "All is well" is the axiom in Voltaire's title: ledger verified. Romans 5:12 and Genesis 3 readings are stated for both sides and left open.
Isaiah 11:9 quotation (ESV) is right, and the wolf and lamb is Isaiah 11:6, paraphrased (see the consider finding on the reference).

"Dozens of psalms": ledger restored (about 50 individual laments; 65 laments in all). Psalm 13:1 (body and Closing Texts), Psalm 88:18 (the psalm's last verse, BSB confirms 18 verses), Matthew 27:46 quoting Psalm 22:1: ESV form, references right.
Holy Saturday kept in the church's calendar: ledger verified (BCP Easter Even). Romans 12:15 in ESV form, comma included.

Wolterstorff: Christian philosopher; Eric died in 1983, aged twenty-five, in a climbing accident in Austria. Search this run: Wikipedia gives 25 and 1983; Philip Yancey's essay gives a spring climb in Austria, during dissertation research in Europe. Lament for a Son (1987) offers no theodicy. "I have no explanation," "I cannot fit these pieces together" (search this run: TTF and the 40th-anniversary edition listing reproduce the passage with both lines) and "Death is awful, demonic." "Mourning bench" is attributed as his phrase. Wolterstorff is living (search this run: professor emeritus at Yale, living in Grand Rapids). Every sentence about him is supported and fair.

988 line ("call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline") and the [Find Help](/help) link: ledger verified, and the wording matches BRIEF.md. No abuse in view, so no reporting line is needed.

John 11:11 (Jesus intends to wake Lazarus), 11:33 and 11:35 quotations, 11:43 (calls him out). Revelation 21:4. Closing Text Romans 8:18. All in ESV form with references. BSB confirms the sense. "The marks of the nails" is grounded in John 20:25-27.
